text: cute asthma UK guidelines recommend beginning with oxygen and a trial of short-acting beta2 agonist given by multiple actuations of an MDI into a large volume spacer, and repeated every 1 to 4 hours if responding. If a poor response is seen, neb- ulised ipratropium is added, and a short course of a high- dose oral corticosteroid (prednisolone 10 mg daily for up to 3 days) may be considered. Global guidelines for acute severe asthma are similar to those in the UK; however, US guidelines for acute severe asthma in adults and children are slightly different.5 Al- though subcutaneous adrenaline or terbutaline has been used in the management of acute severe asthma in the USA, the guidelines suggest that the parenteral use of beta2 agonists is of unproven value. Moreover, in contrast to the UK the intravenous use of xanthines is not recommended. In compiling the UK guidelines the British Thoracic Soci- ety has taken the view that although most patients on max- imal doses of nebulised beta2 agonists and corticosteroids derive no additional benefit from intravenous aminophyl- line, some could obtain additional bronchodilatation; intravenous aminophylline was therefore recommended for patients with life-threatening unresponsive acute asth- ma attacks;6 some evidence in children,50 although not in adults,51 supports this. In contrast, the most recent US guidelines issued by the National Asthma Education and Prevention Program do not recommend the use of xan- thines as they are considered to offer no benefit over the optimal use of inhaled short-acting beta2 agonists and in- creases the frequency of adverse effects.5 In consequence, in the US guidelines, adult patients whose asthma cannot be managed with oxygen, inhaled short-acting beta2 agonists and antimuscarinics, and systemic corticosteroids may be considered for treatment with intravenous magne- sium sulfate or nebulisation with a mixture of helium and oxygen (heliox) in order to avoid intubation and mechani- cal ventilation. UK guidelines consider there is no evi- dence to support the use of heliox; a meta-analysis52 con- cluded that the existing evidence on heliox failed to show a clear benefit, and although lung function might be im- proved in the most severe acute asthma patients, the number and size of studies available for analysis was small and the quality variable. OTHER ASPECTS OF ASTHMA MANAGEMENT Other therapeutic approaches for the management of asth- ma are currently under investigation. Ultra-long-acting beta2 agonists under development such as carmoterol, GSK-159797 (TD-3327), and indacaterol are suitable for once daily use, leading to increased convenience for pa- tients.53 Carbamazepine has shown potential as a treat- ment for asthma in addition to regular asthma therapy;54 improved lung function and fewer exacerbations have been reported
